questions.stem: The CD8+ T cell kills the virus-infected cell using the receptor-ligand pair and downstream caspase shown, without releasing cytotoxic granules. This represents which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A perforin-independent (death-receptor) pathway of cytotoxic killing

explanation.summary: FasL on the CTL engages Fas on the target, activating caspase-3 and apoptosis. This death-receptor pathway is an alternative to perforin/granzyme granule exocytosis and does not require granule contents.
explanation.whyCorrect: FasL on the CTL engages Fas on the target, activating caspase-3 and apoptosis. This death-receptor pathway is an alternative to perforin/granzyme granule exocytosis and does not require granule contents.

questions.stem: On this forward blood typing card, the sample agglutinates (clumps) with anti-A and anti-D reagents but stays smooth with anti-B and the control. What is the blood type?

explanation.summary: Agglutination occurs when a reagent antibody binds a matching red-cell antigen. Clumping with anti-A indicates the A antigen; clumping with anti-D (anti-Rh) indicates Rh(D) positivity; no reaction with anti-B excludes the B antigen. The type is therefore A positive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Agglutination occurs when a reagent antibody binds a matching red-cell antigen. Clumping with anti-A indicates the A antigen; clumping with anti-D (anti-Rh) indicates Rh(D) positivity; no reaction with anti-B excludes the B antigen. The type is therefore A positive.

questions.stem: Etanercept neutralizes TNF-alpha, as shown, but structurally it is not an antibody. What is etanercept?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A soluble TNF-receptor-IgG Fc fusion protein (decoy receptor)

choices.label: B
choices.text: An antisense oligonucleotide against TNF mRNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: A humanized monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha

explanation.summary: Etanercept is a fusion protein linking the extracellular ligand-binding portion of the p75 TNF receptor to the Fc region of human IgG1. It acts as a soluble decoy that binds circulating TNF-alpha, preventing it from activating cell-surface TNF receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Etanercept is a fusion protein linking the extracellular ligand-binding portion of the p75 TNF receptor to the Fc region of human IgG1. It acts as a soluble decoy that binds circulating TNF-alpha, preventing it from activating cell-surface TNF receptors.

questions.stem: This figure contrasts humoral and cell-mediated immunity. A patient with a defect in cytotoxic T lymphocytes would be MOST susceptible to which category of pathogens?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intracellular microbes such as viruses replicating within infected cells

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic (CD8+) T lymphocytes kill host cells harboring intracellular pathogens, especially viruses. Humoral immunity (antibodies) handles extracellular microbes and toxins. Thus a CTL defect chiefly impairs defense against intracellular/viral infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytotoxic (CD8+) T lymphocytes kill host cells harboring intracellular pathogens, especially viruses. Humoral immunity (antibodies) handles extracellular microbes and toxins. Thus a CTL defect chiefly impairs defense against intracellular/viral infections.

questions.stem: The bilaminar embryo shown develops a primitive streak and primitive node. What key process do these structures initiate?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neurulation - closure of the neural tube

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gastrulation - formation of the three germ layers

explanation.summary: Epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to generate endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm during gastrulation. The primitive node organizes the body axis; neural tube closure (neurulation) occurs afterward.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to generate endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm during gastrulation. The primitive node organizes the body axis; neural tube closure (neurulation) occurs afterward.

questions.stem: The developing embryo shown forms pharyngeal (branchial) arches and pouches. The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to which primary lymphoid organ?

explanation.summary: The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Failure of third/fourth pouch development causes DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia with T-cell deficiency and hypocalcemia).
explanation.whyCorrect: The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Failure of third/fourth pouch development causes DiGeorge syndrome (thymic aplasia with T-cell deficiency and hypocalcemia).

questions.stem: The right-hand histology section shows an organ with an outer cortex, an inner medulla, and eosinophilic whorled keratinized structures within the medulla. Which organ is this?

explanation.summary: The whorled eosinophilic Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla are characteristic of the thymus, where developing T cells undergo positive selection (cortex) and negative selection (medulla). The left diagram shows its pharyngeal arch/pouch origin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The whorled eosinophilic Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla are characteristic of the thymus, where developing T cells undergo positive selection (cortex) and negative selection (medulla). The left diagram shows its pharyngeal arch/pouch origin.

questions.stem: In this peripheral blood smear, identify the largest leukocyte, which has abundant blue-gray cytoplasm and a folded, kidney-shaped (indented) nucleus.

explanation.summary: Monocytes are the largest circulating leukocytes, with a folded reniform nucleus and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm. They migrate into tissues to become macrophages. The smaller multilobed cells present are neutrophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monocytes are the largest circulating leukocytes, with a folded reniform nucleus and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm. They migrate into tissues to become macrophages. The smaller multilobed cells present are neutrophils.

questions.stem: In this blood smear, identify the granulocyte with a bilobed nucleus packed with coarse red-orange (eosinophilic) granules.

explanation.summary: Eosinophils have a bilobed nucleus and large red-orange granules. They defend against helminths and participate in allergic (type I hypersensitivity) reactions; their granules contain major basic protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eosinophils have a bilobed nucleus and large red-orange granules. They defend against helminths and participate in allergic (type I hypersensitivity) reactions; their granules contain major basic protein.

questions.stem: This diagram shows an antibody built from five four-chain monomer units held together in a radial arrangement by a central joining (J) chain and disulfide bonds. Which immunoglobulin isotype has this structure?

explanation.summary: A pentamer of five monomers linked by a J chain is the classic structure of secreted IgM, giving it 10 potential antigen-binding sites and making it a highly efficient complement activator. IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary response. Secretory IgA is a dimer with a secretory component; IgG, IgE, and IgD circulate as monomers.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pentamer of five monomers linked by a J chain is the classic structure of secreted IgM, giving it 10 potential antigen-binding sites and making it a highly efficient complement activator. IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary response. Secretory IgA is a dimer with a secretory component; IgG, IgE, and IgD circulate as monomers.

questions.stem: This figure follows B-cell development from a hematopoietic stem cell through pro-B, pre-B, and immature B stages in the bone marrow, then into the circulation as a mature naive B cell. The mature naive B cell shown co-expresses surface IgM together with which other immunoglobulin isotype?

explanation.summary: During antigen-independent development in the bone marrow, the pre-B cell expresses a heavy chain and the immature B cell expresses a complete surface IgM (BCR). As it matures and enters the periphery, the naive B cell co-expresses surface IgM and IgD (produced by alternative splicing of the same heavy-chain transcript). Switching to IgG, IgA, or IgE occurs only later, after antigen encounter and class-switch recombination.

As it matures and enters the periphery, the naive B cell co-expresses surface IgM and IgD (produced by alternative splicing of the same heavy-chain transcript). Switching to IgG, IgA, or IgE occurs only later, after antigen encounter and class-switch recombination.

questions.stem: This figure traces the continuous recirculation of lymphocytes among blood, the thoracic duct, secondary lymphoid organs (lymph node and spleen), and mucosal tissues. Through which specialized vascular structure do naive lymphocytes leave the blood to enter a lymph node?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The central arteriole of the white pulp

explanation.summary: Naive lymphocytes exit the blood into lymph nodes by crossing high endothelial venules, using L-selectin, chemokine, and integrin interactions to home into the node. If they do not encounter antigen, they leave via the efferent lymphatic, which drains toward the thoracic duct and back into the blood, sustaining continuous surveillance. Afferent lymphatics carry antigen and dendritic cells into the node, not blood-borne lymphocytes.
